newsitem.title: FRANCE: Socialists query Renault on plant closure.
newsitem.headline: Socialists query Renault on plant closure.

text.p: France's new Socialist leaders are urging Renault to consider alternatives to closing a plant in Belgium, but the carmaker repeated on Tuesday it had no choice.

"It seems what is needed, and it's what the factory's staff are seeking, is the opening of negotiations and discussions, which hasn't been done," said Elisabeth Guigou, tipped to become the European Affairs minister in a new Socialist government.
Her comments to RTL radio came as Renault met with its European works council to discuss the closure of the Vilvoorde plant which sparked an outcry when it was announced in February.
Renault called the meeting after courts ruled it could not close the plant until it convened the European works council.
Its managers reiterated that the closure was essential not only to reduce costs, but also to streamline the company's money-losing car assembly operations in Europe.

They expect the new government will concede when it looks carefully at the situation that tough measures are needed to save Renault, which lost 5.25 billion francs ($901.2 million) last year and is struggling to break even this year.
Its position was bolstered by dismal car sales data showing a drop of 23 percent in May and a similar fall on the year.
Renault's stock rose 2.13 percent on the bourse on expectations the government will not block its restructuring.

But the unions hope their proposals, which were given short shrift by France's reform-minded conservatives, will get a more sympathetic hearing from the new Socialist-led government which campaigned on providing jobs.
"The European works council is asking that the Renault board ... and the annual general meeting on June 10 order a halt to the closure," the European works council said in a statement.
Five of Renault's 15 directors represent the French state's 46 percent stake. The staff have three representatives, and union leaders hope to line up a majority opposed to the closure.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said just before the election that his party would ask Renault to look for ways to keep the plant open. A spokesman for the new government said on Monday it would discuss the planned closure with Renault.
"We saw a brutal decision come down and, in our opinion, all the possibilities had not been explored," Guigou said.
The unions propose to save the plant by reducing work-weeks and have asked for an independent expert's opinion.
"We want the government to use Renault as a showcase on how to save jobs by reducing work-weeks," said Emmanuel Couvreur of the Socialist-led CFDT union.
He said the union had presented a plan to shorten work-weeks that would not raise production costs over a five-year period.
But Renault says shorter work-weeks are not a solution.

Michel de Virville, secretary general in charge of staff and legal affairs, said reducing work-weeks under the Robien law, which provides lower charges for companies preserving jobs by cutting hours, would not save as much money as the closure. The company estimates the shutdown would save 850 million francs.

More important, de Virville said, shorter work-weeks would not achieve Renault's goal of bringing its scattered production operations in line with those of its competitors in Europe. It produces 125,000 cars on average per plant, compared with over 200,000 at Ford, Opel and Volkswagen.

De Virville said the closure would also cut logistical and equipment costs at Renault, which produces many of its small models in several plants. The Clio, for instance, is built at five sites, including Vilvoorde.
Renault, which has been hammered by a price war in Europe, estimates its share of the overcapacity plaguing the market at around 200,000 cars a day, roughly equal to one plant's output.
Its objective now is to negotiate as many internal transfers and early retirements as possible among the 2,900 or so employees left at Vilvoorde, which has stopped production.

Roughly a quarter would be eligible for early retirement programmes, 600-700 are highly skilled and could find jobs elsewhere and work might be found for some 500 others at suppliers in the region in elsewhere in the company.
But Renault also plans to cut nearly 2,800 jobs in France this year and reduce staff by similar numbers in coming years.
On Monday, the Peugeot car division of rival PSA Peugeot Citroen said it would shed 2,816 jobs. ($ = 5.825 French Francs)
